builder_plan.scenario: Your inference service slows down when several customers send requests together.
builder_plan.change: Replay a recorded request trace with only the proposed serving policy changed.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current scheduler on the same model and hardware.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Requests meeting your latency target, throughput, failures, and cost per successful request.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
summary: MotionServe replaces per-robot dedicated GPUs or naive shared-GPU dispatch of VLA policies with LoRA-shared backbones plus coordinated observation triggering (MotionExec) and slack-aware batch scheduling (SlackBatch). It costs the engineering complexity of a custom scheduler tied to action-chunk semantics and requires LoRA-compatible policies sharing a frozen backbone, which constrains model and adaptation choices. It can fail when GPU-work estimates are inaccurate or motion-structure triggers misfire, since exhausted execution slack produces robot stalls and early observation can cause disruptive replanning that lowers task success; results are validated only in simulation on two VLA models.
rationale: The system addresses shared-GPU serving of many concurrent robot policies on an H200 with 96 simulated robots, a workload far removed from the reader's single-GPU, non-robotics constraints, so it is relevant context but not adoptable.
technique: Slack-aware batching for shared-GPU robot policy serving

claims.statement: MotionServe replaces per-robot dedicated GPUs or naive shared-GPU dispatch of VLA policies with LoRA-shared backbones plus coordinated observation triggering (MotionExec) and slack-aware batch scheduling (SlackBatch). It costs the engineering complexity of a custom scheduler tied to action-chunk semantics and requires LoRA-compatible policies sharing a frozen backbone, which constrains model and adaptation choices. It can fail when GPU-work estimates are inaccurate or motion-structure triggers misfire, since exhausted execution slack produces robot stalls and early observation can cause disruptive replanning that lowers task success; results are validated only in simulation on two VLA models.

At 96 simulated robots on one H200, reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points over each model's lowest-stall baseline; LoRA backbone sharing cuts weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
